scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: PANIC from the night shift -- an alert popped up and
now everyone thinks one of the big routers in the middle of the network has
gone wrong overnight, but I don't know which one. Everything crossing the
middle is dying somewhere. Could someone look at it and tell us it's fixed!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected component is r1's eth0 interface IP address, which is misconfigured with 12.1.1.1/8 instead of the correct 1.1.1.1/8. r2's eth0 on the same collision domain A carries 1.1.1.2/8 (subnet 1.0.0.0/8). Because /8 masks are in use, r1 and r2 land in completely different subnets (12.0.0.0/8 vs 1.0.0.0/8) even though they share the same Layer-2 segment.

OSPF on a broadcast network validates that a received Hello comes from a router in the same subnet before accepting it as a neighbor. r1 sends Hellos sourced from 12.1.1.1/8; r2 rejects them (wrong subnet) and vice versa. The result is confirmed: r1 eth0 has 0 OSPF neighbors, r2 eth0 has 0 OSPF neighbors, and a direct L3 ping between the two on that segment loses 100% of packets.

The direct backbone link A between r1 and r2 is completely unused. Both routers are forced to route all traffic to each other through r3, making r3 the sole transit point for everything between r1's half of the backbone (including Area 3 — r11, r12, r13) and r2's half (including stub Area 4 — r10). Backbone redundancy is eliminated. r1's OSPF config also spuriously advertises 12.0.0.0/8 into the domain, which is a phantom network no other router can usefully reach.

Root cause: r1 eth0 was assigned 12.1.1.1/8 instead of 1.1.1.1/8, creating an IP subnet mismatch with r2 on shared domain A and destroying the direct OSPF adjacency.

Fix: Change r1 eth0 from 12.1.1.1/8 to 1.1.1.1/8, and update r1's OSPF network statement from `network 12.0.0.0/8 area 0` to `network 1.0.0.0/8 area 0`. This restores the r1–r2 adjacency, re-establishes backbone redundancy, and removes the spurious 12.0.0.0/8 advertisement.

per_axis.rationale: The diagnosis omits any mention that R6/R7 are up with a Full adjacency and that PC0 can reach PC12 across the core; it instead focuses only on an r1/r2 misconfiguration.

The agent's claims are directly supported by observed command outputs (ip addrs, OSPF neighbors, interface pings, running configs) and its inferences (address mismatch → no adjacency → traffic detour) follow logically. The investigation covers the essential checks to justify the misconfiguration diagnosis, with only minor truncation of some outputs.
